title: Alkanes
learningObjective: know the general formula for alkanes; explain why alkanes are classified as saturated hydrocarbons; understand how to draw the structural and displayed formulae for alkanes with up to five carbon atoms in the molecule, and to name the unbranched-chain isomers; describe the reactions of alkanes with halogens in the presence of ultraviolet radiation, limited to mono-substitution knowledge of reaction mechanisms is not required

sections.title: Alkanes
sections.markdown:
---


The hydrocarbons that emerge from the fractional distillation of
crude oil (u4:c23) are mainly **[[alkane]]s** — and this chapter is
devoted to them, because they are the simplest family of
[[hydrocarbon]]s in chemistry. Every molecule in the family is built
from just two kinds of bond: carbon–carbon single bonds and
carbon–hydrogen single bonds. Nothing else. That one structural fact
explains almost everything you are about to read: why the family has
a neat formula, why its members behave in similar ways, why the
family is described as unreactive, and why — despite that — every
alkane will burn. The structures and reactions of these compounds
build directly on the bonding and formula work from the
introduction to organic chemistry (u4:c22).

Start with the family portrait. The small alkanes — methane, ethane,
propane, butane — are gases at room temperature, and their most
important job is the one happening around you right now: they burn
as fuels. Methane is the major component of natural gas, the
fuel that likely heats your home; ethane and propane are present in
small quantities in natural gas too, and both are important
constituents of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) from crude oil
distillation. The first five members of the family are laid out in
the table below — learn to read it, because it is the map of
everything else in this chapter.

| Name | Molecular formula | Structural formula |
|------|-------------------|--------------------|
| methane | CH₄ | CH₄ |
| ethane | C₂H₆ | CH₃CH₃ |
| propane | C₃H₈ | CH₃CH₂CH₃ |
| butane | C₄H₁₀ | CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ |
| pentane | C₅H₁₂ | CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ |

Two columns of that table deserve a second look. The **molecular
formula** counts atoms: C₃H₈ tells you a propane molecule contains
3 carbon atoms and 8 hydrogen atoms, and nothing about how they are
joined. The **structural formula** shows the order of the chain:
CH₃CH₂CH₃ says carbon–carbon–carbon, with the hydrogen atoms
attached along it. A third representation exists too — the
**displayed formula** — in which every single bond is drawn as an
explicit line and every atom is shown. For methane it is a central C
with four H atoms each joined to it by one line (H–C–H on top and
bottom, H on each side); for ethane it is H–C–H above and below each
of the two carbon atoms joined by a central C–C line; and each
further member lengthens the carbon backbone by one carbon, with
hydrogen atoms filling every remaining bond. Drawing displayed
formulae for these first five alkanes, and naming the straight-chain
members, is a skill this chapter trains — specification statement
4.21 asks for exactly that, up to five carbon atoms.

Now the word that will follow the family for the rest of the
chapter: **saturated**. The alkanes are [[saturated-hydrocarbon]]s
because they contain only C–C single bonds and have no double (C=C)
or triple (C≡C) bonds anywhere in the molecule. Every carbon atom is
using all four of its bonds on four neighbours, and there is no
double bond anywhere waiting to react. Keep the definition in
exactly that shape — single bonds only — because it is the version
the mark scheme rewards.

:::key-point
The alkanes are **saturated hydrocarbons**: they contain only C–C
single bonds and no double (C=C) or triple (C≡C) bonds. A helpful
way of thinking about it is that the alkanes are *saturated with
hydrogen* — they carry the maximum number of hydrogen atoms possible
for their number of carbon atoms. The thinking aid is for your
understanding; the exam definition is the single-bonds sentence.
:::

:::prior-knowledge
This chapter assumes you have already studied the introduction to
organic chemistry (u4:c22): hydrocarbons, the C–C and C–H bonding
skeleton, and how organic formulae are written and read. The
covalent bonding model itself comes from u1:c07 and u1:c08, and the
way a molecule's size controls the strength of its
intermolecular forces — which returns in Section 5 of this
lesson to explain a beautiful property trend — was first met there.
The crude oil story (u4:c23) supplies the starting material: it is
the alkanes' industrial source.
:::

:::cross-curricular
The fuel role of the small alkanes is an energy story as much as a
chemistry one. Burning methane in a boiler, propane in a camp stove
and the LPG mixture in a rural kitchen are all the same chemical
event — C–C and C–H bonds being replaced by stronger C=O and O–H
bonds — releasing the difference as heat. Physics calls it
combustion enthalpy; geography maps where the gas pipelines run; and
Section 7 of this lesson puts the equations on the table.
:::

:::exam-hint
When a question asks *why are alkanes classified as saturated
hydrocarbons*, the mark scheme wants the bonding statement: **they
contain only single bonds** (C–C and C–H), with no C=C or C≡C
double or triple bonds. Do not write "they are full of hydrogen" or
"saturated with hydrogen" — that is a thinking aid, not a
definition, and it earns nothing on its own. If you want to use the
hydrogen-counting idea at all, bolt it on *after* the bonding
sentence, never instead of it.
:::

:::misconception
"Saturated means the molecule holds as much hydrogen as it can, so
it cannot react." The second half of that sentence is wrong twice
over. Saturated describes the *bonding* (single bonds only), not a
reaction limit — and every alkane burns readily, as Section 7 will
show. The word describes structure, not laziness: alkanes are
*saturated* yet still undergo two important reactions.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you define a hydrocarbon in one sentence with the word *only*
doing its job? Can you state why alkanes are saturated in bonding
language — single C–C and C–H bonds, no C=C, no C≡C? Can you write
the molecular and structural formulae of the first five alkanes from
memory, and sketch the displayed formula of methane and ethane with
every bond drawn? If all four are yes, the rest of the chapter is
downhill.
:::

sections.title: Isomers of alkanes
sections.markdown:
Hand any two chemists the same molecular formula and they can build
different molecules from it — and that possibility has a name. An
[[isomer]] is a compound that has the same [[molecular-formula]] as
another compound but a different [[structural-formula]]. The atoms
are identical in kind and number; only their connection pattern
differs. Isomerism is one of the reasons organic chemistry has
millions of compounds while inorganic chemistry has thousands: with
a few dozen atoms to arrange, the number of legal connection
patterns explodes fast.

The first three alkanes have no isomers at all. There is exactly
one way to join one carbon to four hydrogens (methane), one way for
two carbons and six hydrogens (ethane), and one way for three
carbons and eight hydrogens (propane) — the carbon atoms have no
choice but to sit in a line. The alkanes in the table back in
Section 1 are therefore all described as **straight-chain alkanes**,
or as having an **unbranched chain**: every carbon atom sits at the
end or in the run of the chain, with no carbon hanging off the
middle of another.

From butane upwards, the choice appears. There are isomers of
butane (C₄H₁₀) and pentane (C₅H₁₂) that have **branched chains** —
chains in which one carbon atom is attached to the middle of the
chain rather than at its end. For butane, the unbranched member
chains all four carbons in a row (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃), while the branched
isomer takes three of the carbons in a chain and hangs the fourth
off the middle one, giving the structural formula CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃.
Pentane has more arrangements still: the straight chain, one
branched form with a single carbon branch on the second carbon
(CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃), and one doubly-branched form where two carbon
branches sit on the middle carbon of a three-carbon backbone
(CH₃C(CH₃)₂CH₃). Each of these is a distinct compound with its own
melting point, boiling point and reaction behaviour, even though
every one of them is C₅H₁₂.

To draw a branched isomer's [[displayed-formula]] correctly, build
the carbon backbone first, count the bonds each carbon still has
spare, and fill every spare bond with a hydrogen atom. A middle
carbon bonded to two chain neighbours has two spare bonds; an end
carbon has three; a carbon carrying a branch has one. When every
carbon shows exactly four bonds and every hydrogen exactly one, the
drawing is right — and the same atom-counting discipline is what
makes the equations in Section 7 come out balanced.

:::key-point
An **isomer** is a compound with the *same* molecular formula but a
*different* structural formula compared with another compound.
Methane, ethane and propane have no isomers; butane and pentane
have branched-chain isomers in which a carbon atom attaches to the
middle of the chain instead of the end.
:::

:::exam-hint
Isomer questions are atom-counting questions in disguise. Before
drawing anything, write the molecular formula and total the atoms —
for C₄H₁₀ that is 4 carbons and 10 hydrogens, no more and no less.
Then draw the unbranched chain, and only then move one carbon to
the middle and re-fill the bonds. Finish by counting every atom in
your drawing against the formula; one hydrogen short or long means
a carbon has the wrong number of bonds, and the examiner will find
it in seconds.
:::

:::misconception
"Isomers are the same compound drawn differently." No — they are
*different compounds* that happen to share a molecular formula.
Straight-chain butane and its branched isomer have different
boiling points, different densities and slightly different
reactivities, because molecule shape controls how strongly
molecules attract each other. If two structures differ in how the
atoms are connected, they are two substances; if they differ only
in how the paper is rotated, they are one.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you define an isomer using both halves of the sentence — same
molecular formula, different structural formula? Can you explain
why propane has no isomers while butane does? And can you draw the
displayed formula of a branched-chain isomer of C₄H₁₀ with all four
bonds on every carbon accounted for? Draw it now before moving on —
the substitution reactions in Section 7 will hand you isomeric
products, and you will want this skill warm.
:::

sections.title: Homologous series
sections.markdown:
The alkanes are not a random pile of similar molecules — they form
a [[homologous-series]], and that phrase has a precise meaning you
are expected to reproduce. A homologous series is a series of
compounds that:

- have the same [[functional-group]];
- have similar chemical properties;
- show a trend (a gradation) in their physical properties;
- can be described by the same [[general-formula]];
- differ from the next member by a –CH₂– unit.

Each bullet is a statement you can test against any family in
organic chemistry, and the alkanes pass all five, which is why they
are called the simplest homologous series. Move from methane to
ethane and you add exactly one –CH₂– unit; move from ethane to
propane, another –CH₂–; every step of the ladder is the same
sized step, and Sections 4 and 5 turn that regularity into a
formula and a property trend respectively.

One honest wrinkle: the alkanes do not really have a functional
group in the way other families do, because they just contain
single C–C and C–H bonds — and that C–C and C–H skeleton is
precisely what all other organic chemistry is built on. Every other
homologous series you will meet (the alkenes of u4:c25, the alcohols
of u4:c26, the carboxylic acids of u4:c27) is the alkane skeleton
with one bond upgraded into a reactive group. That is why the
alkanes are the right family to learn first: they are the plain
fabric on which all the embroidery of organic chemistry is stitched.

:::exam-hint
When a question asks about a homologous series, the safest answer
writes about the *properties* — the second and third bullets of the
definition list above. Questions often do not award separate marks
for "the same functional group" and "similar chemical properties"
as two independent statements, and a stronger single sentence earns
them together: **they have similar chemical properties because they
have the same functional group**. If a third mark is available, add
the trend statement — a gradation in physical properties as the
molecules increase in size by –CH₂– units.
:::

:::key-point
A **homologous series** is a family of compounds with the same
functional group, similar chemical properties, a gradation in
physical properties, one shared general formula, and consecutive
members that differ by a single –CH₂– unit. The alkanes are the
simplest example — their "functional group" is just the C–C and
C–H single-bond skeleton itself.
:::

:::misconception
"Every organic family must have an obviously reactive functional
group, so alkanes cannot be a homologous series." They can and
they are. The series definition asks for the *same* group across
all members — and for alkanes that shared feature is the saturated
C–C/C–H single-bond skeleton, present identically in every member.
The consequence is real and examinable: with no reactive group to
attack, alkanes are fairly unreactive, which is exactly the
chemical similarity the definition predicts.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you reproduce all five bullets of the homologous-series
definition without peeking? Can you deploy the one-sentence
properties answer — similar chemical properties *because* the same
functional group? And can you explain why the alkane skeleton
counts as the family's shared feature even though alkanes have no
reactive group? These sentences are the family passport: alkenes,
alcohols and acids will all demand them again.
:::

sections.title: Members of a homologous series have the same general formula
sections.markdown:
Because every step up the alkane ladder adds exactly one carbon and
two hydrogens — the –CH₂– unit from the series definition in
Section 3 — the whole family collapses into one expression. For the
alkanes, if there are *n* carbons there are 2*n* + 2 hydrogens,
which gives the [[general-formula]]:

**CₙH₂ₙ₊₂**

Substitute any whole number for *n* and the formula hands you a real
alkane. One carbon (n = 1) gives CH₄, methane; two give C₂H₆,
ethane; three give C₃H₈, propane. Check it against the table in
Section 1 and every row agrees — that is what it means for a
[[homologous-series]] to have a general formula. The formula works
because each member differs from the next by a –CH₂– unit: grow the
carbon count by one and the hydrogen count grows by exactly two,
which is the 2*n* + 2 pattern stated in algebra.

:::worked-example
Find the [[molecular-formula]] of the alkane with 15 carbon atoms.

The general formula says hydrogens = 2*n* + 2, and here *n* = 15.
So hydrogens = (2 × 15) + 2 = 32, and the answer is **C₁₅H₃₂**.
Verify the method on a case you can count by hand first: for
propane, *n* = 3 gives (2 × 3) + 2 = 8 hydrogens — C₃H₈, exactly as
the table in Section 1 shows. The same one-line method produces any
member of the family, which is why exam questions like to name
alkanes with large carbon counts: undecane (11 carbons) is C₁₁H₂₄
without a table in sight.
:::

The power of a general formula runs both ways. Given a name and a
carbon count, it produces the formula (the worked example above);
given a formula, it confirms family membership. Any compound whose
formula fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ for some whole number *n* is an alkane — the
formula is a fingerprint. An alkane with 11
carbons must be C₁₁H₂₄; a formula like C₃H₆ fails the test
(2 × 3 + 2 = 8, not 6), and that failure is meaningful: C₃H₆ is not
a member of *this* family (it belongs to the alkenes of u4:c25, and
the missing two hydrogens are exactly what its C=C double bond
implies).

The same regularity is visible in the pictures. Draw the displayed
formulae of the three smallest alkanes — methane, ethane, propane —
side by side and each one is the previous drawing with one more
carbon inserted into the backbone and two more hydrogens packed on:
methane a single carbon crowned with four hydrogens, ethane two
carbons sharing one bond, propane three carbons sharing two. Each
member differs from the next by exactly a –CH₂– unit, which is the
structural reason the formula arithmetic works.

:::cross-curricular
The general formula is algebra wearing a chemistry coat. The
expression C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> is a function: input an
integer, output a compound. This is the same move mathematics makes
when it writes the *n*th term of a sequence — here the sequence is
CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈, C₄H₁₀, C₅H₁₂, … and the "term-to-term rule" is
"add CH₂". When you meet formulae like this across science, you are
looking at one of the deepest ideas in the subject: a family too
large to list can be captured in one line of algebra.
:::

:::misconception
"A formula that fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ always describes exactly one
compound, so butane must be a single substance." The general formula counts
atoms; it does not fix how they are joined. C₄H₁₀ fits the
formula perfectly and is TWO compounds — the straight chain and its branched
isomer of Section 2. The formula is a family fingerprint, not a structural
diagram: it narrows the world to the alkanes, and the isomer skill then
distinguishes the members within it.
:::

:::exam-hint
The general formula is your marking-proof checking tool. After
balancing any alkane combustion equation in Section 7 or answering
any "write the molecular formula of ..." item, run the formula
through CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: if your alkane's hydrogen
count does not equal twice the carbon count plus two, something is
wrong — a mis-drawn structure, a lost subscript or an unbalanced
equation upstream. Questions love the "undecane" style (a named
alkane with a carbon count you must decode from the name, not the
table): undecane has 11 carbons (uni- = one, dec- = ten), so its
formula is C₁₁H₂₄ by the general formula alone.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you state the general formula of the alkanes and explain what
*n* stands for? Can you derive the formula of the alkane with 15
carbons in one line of arithmetic? Can you use the formula in
reverse — to test whether C₃H₆ could be an alkane — and say which
family it actually belongs to? And can you connect the formula back
to the –CH₂– unit rule from the homologous-series definition? Four
yeses here and 4.19 is banked.
:::

sections.title: Members of a homologous series show a trend in physical properties
sections.markdown:
Because the members of a [[homologous-series]] grow in size in a
regular way — one –CH₂– unit at a time — their physical properties
change in a regular way too, and the clearest example is the
[[boiling-point]]. Plot the boiling points of the first eight alkanes
against the number of carbon atoms and the points rise in a smooth,
regular sweep: methane boils near −162 °C, and each extra carbon
lifts the boiling point a step further. This graph-like pattern is
what the series definition means by a **trend (gradation) in
physical properties** — no member is out of line, because no member
differs from its neighbours except by the same –CH₂– unit.

The trend sorts the family into states for you. The first four
alkanes — methane, ethane, propane and butane — are gases at room
temperature (about 25 °C). All the other alkanes you are likely to
meet at International GCSE are liquids. Solids start to appear at
about C₁₈H₃₈, where the molecules are so large that the attractions
between them rarely let go at room temperature. That is why the
fuel table from Section 1 reads the way it does: the small alkanes
are gases burned as fuels (natural gas, LPG), the mid-sized members
are the liquid fuels of the petrol and diesel fractions, and the
giants are the waxy solids of the heavier fractions.

The root cause of the trend is the same force you met in covalent
bonding (u1:c08): [[intermolecular-forces]], the attractions between
one molecule and its neighbours. As the molecules become bigger,
the strength of these attractions increases — a bigger molecule
presents more surface to its neighbours and gathers more of their
attractions. More energy therefore has to be put in to break the
attractions between one molecule and the ones around it, and one
effect of that is the one the graph shows: the boiling points
increase in a regular way. Nothing about the covalent bonds *inside*
the molecule changes as the family grows — it is the
between-molecule attractions that strengthen, and the boiling point
merely reports the energy bill.

:::key-point
The boiling points of the alkanes increase regularly with molecule
size because bigger molecules have stronger
[[intermolecular-forces]]; more energy is needed to separate
neighbouring molecules, so bigger alkanes boil higher. The first
four alkanes are gases at room temperature, the IGCSE-relevant
mid-range members are liquids, and solids appear at about C₁₈H₃₈.
:::

:::exam-hint
Trend questions pay two marks for two statements, so always write
both: the *direction* (boiling point increases as molecules get
bigger) and the *cause* (stronger intermolecular forces of
attraction between the larger molecules, needing more energy to
overcome). Writing only the direction earns half; writing the cause
with the wrong direction earns nothing. And keep the force
*between* molecules — a sentence that breaks covalent bonds during
boiling loses the mark it was aiming at.
:::

:::misconception
"When a big alkane boils, its covalent bonds break and that is why
more energy is needed." No bond breaks. Boiling separates
*molecules from molecules*, and the only thing being overcome is
the intermolecular force of attraction between neighbouring
molecules. The C–C and C–H covalent bonds inside each molecule
survive the process untouched — the same molecule that was a vapour
condenses back to a liquid with its bonds intact. Energy bills
differ between sizes because the *between-molecule* attractions
differ, not because the molecules themselves change.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you state the direction of the boiling-point trend across the
first eight alkanes? Can you name the state of the first four
members at room temperature, the state of the mid-range members,
and the size at which solids appear? And can you explain the trend
in a two-step cause chain — bigger molecules, stronger
intermolecular forces, more energy to separate neighbours? That
cause-chain is the same one that sorted crude oil's fractions into
a boiling-order column (u4:c23, statement 4.10) — here it reappears
inside a single family, which is why the alkane ladder boils
smoothly instead of in jumps.
:::

sections.title: Members of a homologous series have similar chemical properties
sections.markdown:
Chemical properties are decided by [[functional-group]]s and bonding.
Since every member of the [[alkane]] family contains exactly the same
bonding — carbon–carbon single bonds and carbon–hydrogen single
bonds and nothing else — every member is going to behave in the
same way chemically. That is the second properties bullet of the
homologous-series definition doing its job: one shared bonding
pattern, one shared reaction behaviour. Learn how one alkane reacts
and you have, to a good approximation, learned them all.

Those strong C–C and C–H single bonds are hard to break, and so the
alkanes are **fairly unreactive** organic compounds — they are
often thought of as being quite inert. The description is
comparative, and the comparison matters. Alkanes are not inert in
the sense that they do not react with anything, like neon does;
rather, they are not very reactive *for organic compounds*, and
they really undergo only two reactions. Those two reactions —
combustion and substitution with halogens — are the whole of the
alkane reaction list at International GCSE, and they are the
business of Section 7.

Why does saturation produce this quietness? A [[saturated-hydrocarbon]]
has no double bond available as a reactive handle. Compare that
with the unsaturated alkenes coming in u4:c25, whose C=C double bond
is electron-rich and eager to attack: every dramatic organic
reaction you will later watch happens at a double bond, and the
alkanes have none. The family's saturation — statement 4.20 — is
therefore not just a structural label but the chemical explanation
of the family's restraint.

:::key-point
The alkanes are **fairly unreactive**: they are not inert in the
sense of never reacting (unlike neon), but they are not very
reactive *for organic compounds*, and they really undergo only two
reactions — combustion, and substitution with halogens. Their
strong C–C and C–H single bonds and the absence of any C=C double
bond explain the restraint.
:::

:::exam-hint
Handle the word *inert* with care — it is a comparison, not an
absolution. If a question says "alkanes are unreactive. Explain
why," the mark scheme wants the bonding argument: strong C–C and
C–H single bonds that are difficult to break, and no reactive
double bond. If a question shows a reaction happening, do not
insist the alkane "cannot react" — it can, and Section 7 gives you
both reactions it does undergo. Match the strength of your claim to
the strength of the evidence in front of you.
:::

:::misconception
"Unreactive means no reactions at all, so alkanes are chemical
dead-ends." The family has exactly two reactions and one of them
powers civilisation. What *unreactive* means here is narrower: few
reactions, and only under specific conditions — high temperature
for combustion, ultraviolet light for substitution. The quietness
is also what makes the reactions that do happen so clean to learn:
two behaviours, memorably different, shared by every member of the
family.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you explain why all alkanes share similar chemical properties
(one bonding pattern, one behaviour)? Can you qualify the word
*inert* correctly — fairly unreactive for organic compounds, not
neon-like? And can you name the two reactions the family really
undergoes before reading the next section? Hold those two names
(combustion, substitution) in mind; Section 7 now earns them their
equations.
:::

sections.title: Two reactions of the alkanes
sections.markdown:
Section 6 promised two reactions; here they both are, with their
equations. All alkanes burn in air or oxygen — that is reaction one.
Alkanes react with halogens in the presence of ultraviolet
radiation — that is reaction two. Everything else you may hear
about alkane chemistry at International GCSE is a variation on
these two themes.

## Combustion

If there is enough oxygen, an alkane burns completely to give
carbon dioxide and water. Two examples, straight from the family:

CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)

2C₂H₆(g) + 7O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l)

If there is not enough oxygen, the combustion is
[[incomplete-combustion]], and you obtain [[carbon-monoxide]] or
carbon (soot) instead of carbon dioxide — with water still
produced:

2C₂H₆(g) + 5O₂(g) → 4CO(g) + 6H₂O(l)

or

2C₂H₆(g) + 3O₂(g) → 4C(s) + 6H₂O(l)

Read the four equations as one story with an oxygen dial. Plenty of
oxygen: every carbon reaches CO₂. Moderate shortage: carbon can
only reach CO. Severe shortage: carbon cannot bond to oxygen at all
and drops out as soot. In every version the hydrogens still end as
water — [[complete-combustion]] and incomplete differ *only* in the
fate of the carbon.

The incomplete products are not academic. Carbon monoxide is the
colourless, odourless gas that binds to haemoglobin in place of
oxygen — the poisoning mechanism you met in the crude oil chapter
(u4:c23) — which is why a flame starved of air in a closed room is
a killer and not just an inconvenience. Soot is the black smoke
that coats the inside of a burner starved of oxygen. The chemistry
of the oxygen dial is the safety story behind every "ventilate the
room" warning on a gas appliance.

Never try to memorise combustion equations — there are as many of
them as there are fuels. Practise deriving them instead: write the
skeleton (fuel + O₂), send every hydrogen to H₂O, then send the
carbons to CO₂, CO or C according to the oxygen available, and
balance the O₂ last. The full method is trained in the formulae and
calculations lessons (u1:c05, u1:c06). Balanced in that order, even
the 15-carbon giants of Section 4 surrender in a minute.

## Substitution

The second reaction swaps an atom instead of burning the molecule.
Alkanes react with halogens in the presence of [[ultraviolet-radiation]]
(UV light), for example from sunlight. A hydrogen atom in the
alkane is replaced by a halogen atom — and because one atom has
been replaced (or *substituted*) by a different one, the reaction
type is called a [[substitution-reaction]].

Watch it happen with methane and bromine. A mixture of methane and
bromine gas is orange, because of the bromine. Leave the mixture in
sunlight and the colour fades: the bromine has been consumed, and a
mixture of bromomethane and hydrogen bromide gases has formed.
The displayed-formula picture of the change is worth building in
your head: a methane molecule with its four C–H bonds stands next
to a Br–Br molecule; the products are the same methane frame with
one H replaced by Br, plus a small H–Br molecule carrying the
displaced hydrogen. In symbols:

CH₄(g) + Br₂(g) → CH₃Br(g) + HBr(g)

An exactly similar reaction happens between ethane and chlorine
exposed to UV light, giving a mixture of chloroethane and hydrogen
chloride gases:

CH₃CH₃(g) + Cl₂(g) → CH₃CH₂Cl(g) + HCl(g)

When only one hydrogen atom is replaced — [[mono-substitution]] —
propane reacting with bromine still manages two organic products,
because the bromine can sit on either of the two end carbons or on
the middle one. The two products are structural isomers of each
other: same molecular formula (C₃H₇Br), different structural
formulae. Products of substitution reactions of alkanes with
halogens are called [[halogenoalkane]]s, named in the format
*x*-haloalkane, where *x* gives the position of the halogen atom in
the longest carbon chain — so bromine reacting with propane gives
1-bromopropane and 2-bromopropane.

One wording trap sits inside that second equation. The HCl(g)
formed is called **hydrogen chloride**, not hydrochloric acid. To
form an acid, hydrogen chloride gas must dissolve in water and
dissociate to form H⁺ ions — the acids story from u2:c16. A dry gas
is not an acid, and writing "hydrochloric acid" beside a (g) state
symbol is a mark surrendered.

:::key-point
The alkanes undergo exactly two reactions. **Combustion**: burning
in oxygen — complete gives CO₂ + H₂O, incomplete (limited oxygen)
gives CO and/or soot, always plus water. **Substitution**: reaction
with a halogen in the presence of UV light, where one hydrogen atom
of the alkane is replaced by one halogen atom.
:::

:::exam-hint
The condition word examiners are hunting in substitution questions
is **ultraviolet radiation** (UV light) — sunlight is the everyday
example. Name it or lose the mark: "heat" and "catalyst" belong to
cracking (u4:c23), not here. And when you name the HCl product,
match the state to the name: HCl(g) is *hydrogen chloride*; only
its aqueous solution is *hydrochloric acid*. Both of these are
one-word, one-mark checks that cost nothing to get right forever.
:::

:::did-you-know
If bromine is in excess, the substitution does not stop at one
hydrogen. The reaction can go on to replace more of the hydrogens
in the methane, and what you obtain is a mixture of CH₃Br,
CH₂Br₂, CHBr₃ and CBr₄ — plus HBr of course. This
multi-substitution chemistry is exactly the kind of thing you will
meet again if you take chemistry further; at International GCSE the
mono-substitution products are the examinable ones.
:::

:::did-you-know
Why does the reaction need UV light at all? The UV radiation splits
halogen molecules into atoms — energy is needed to break the covalent
bond between the two halogen atoms. The atoms formed are called
**free radicals**, because of the unpaired electrons they carry;
these very reactive species are what go on to attack the otherwise
unreactive alkane. Without the light, the bromine stays as the
orange Br₂ molecules you started with.
:::

:::misconception
"Alkanes react with bromine water and decolorise it — that's the
substitution test." That is the *alkenes'* test (u4:c25), and it
happens rapidly in the dark without any special condition. Alkanes
need pure halogen *and* UV light, and they substitute slowly —
which is precisely why "no rapid decolourising of bromine water"
behaves as the negative result that distinguishes a saturated
hydrocarbon from an unsaturated one. Mixing up the two conditions
is one of the classic organic-chemistry mark losses.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write the complete-combustion equation for methane — and
derive, not recall, the ethane one? Can you state the two products
of incomplete combustion and why one of them is dangerous to
humans? Can you give the exact condition for the substitution
reaction, name the products when methane meets bromine, and explain
why the hydrogen chloride formed is not called an acid? That is the
complete alkane reaction list — two reactions, six equations' worth
of variations, one family.
:::

sections.title: Chapter 24 questions
sections.markdown:
You now hold the complete [[alkane]] story. The family is the simplest
set of [[hydrocarbon]]s: C–C and C–H single bonds only
([[saturated-hydrocarbon]], 4.20), organised as a homologous series
whose members step up by –CH₂– units, all obeying one
[[general-formula]] (4.19), learnable through the first five named
members and their molecular, structural and displayed formulae
(4.21). Physically the members grade smoothly — gases up to butane,
liquids through the IGCSE range, solids from about C₁₈H₃₈ — because
bigger molecules mean stronger intermolecular forces. Chemically
the family is quiet: two reactions only, combustion (complete and
incomplete, with the [[carbon-monoxide]] hazard) and UV-light
[[substitution-reaction]] with halogens (4.22). Every specification
statement of this chapter — 4.19 to 4.22 — has been taught, and
each now joins the platform question bank through the links below,
with practice items keyed to exactly those statements.

Before opening the bank, audit yourself against the chapter's core
moves. Can you write the saturated-hydrocarbon definition in
bonding language? Can you apply CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ forwards (formula from
carbon count) and backwards (family membership from formula)? Can
you draw a branched-chain [[isomer]] with every carbon's four bonds
accounted for? Can you derive — not recall — a complete-combustion
equation for any alkane you are handed, and state what changes when
the oxygen runs short? Can you name the condition for substitution
and explain why its gaseous acid fume is not "an acid"? Any wobble
is a section to revisit, not a reason to start over.

The question bank for this chapter trains a predictable set of
shapes, so rehearse the moves rather than the answers. Definition
items open the set: the saturated-hydrocarbon explanation in
bonding language, exactly as Section 1 drilled it. Formula items
then hand you named alkanes whose molecular formulae must come from
the general formula alone — undecane and friends — sometimes with a
physical-state prediction attached, which Section 5's trend answers
without a table. Drawing items ask for pairs of isomers of a given
alkane, where Section 2's backbone-then-fill method and atom count
earn the marks. Equation items run the full combustion dial — a
complete equation, then an incomplete one, then the *why* behind
the hazard of the carbon-monoxide product — and the substitution
block checks the condition word, the reaction type, a displayed
equation and the name of the organic product. A closing item asks
for two isomeric products from a single mono-substitution of a
branched precursor — the isomer skill and the substitution skill
shaking hands. The shapes are the chapter; the fuel names are just
costumes.

:::exam-hint
Balance the practice time against the mark structure: the
definition and formula items are fast marks — bank them first and
refuse to overthink them. The drawing items are where precision
pays: draw the backbone, fill the bonds, count the atoms, then
move on. For the equation items, derive in the fixed order
(hydrogens to water first, carbons second, balance oxygen last) —
the order never changes, and neither do the marks it earns. And in
substitution items, write the condition *before* the equation; it
is the one-mark sentence people forget under time pressure.
:::

:::misconception
"The question bank rewards knowing the printed answers." It rewards
knowing the *chemistry* — the same reaction can be asked about
through a different fuel, a different halogen or a different
product, and a memorised answer to a different question will not
fit. That is why this lesson trained methods (the general-formula
substitution, the backbone-and-fill drawing routine, the
derive-don't-memorise combustion order, the oxygen dial) rather
than specific answers. If you can run the method, the question's
costume does not matter.
:::

:::summary
- **Alkanes and saturation (4.20)**: the simplest hydrocarbon
  family — C–C and C–H single bonds only, no C=C or C≡C; saturated
  because every bond is single; fairly unreactive as a
  consequence, with strong bonds and no reactive handle.
- **The general formula (4.19)**: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — n carbons carry
  2n + 2 hydrogens; each member differs from the next by –CH₂–;
  membership is proved by fitting the formula; undecane is
  C₁₁H₂₄ by one line of arithmetic.
- **The first five members (4.21)**: methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆,
  propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀, pentane C₅H₁₂ — draw structural and
  displayed formulae up to five carbons and name the unbranched
  chain; isomers share a molecular formula but differ in
  structural formula (butane and pentane have branched forms).
- **The homologous series frame**: same functional group (the
  C–C/C–H skeleton), similar chemical properties, a gradation in
  physical properties, one general formula, –CH₂– steps.
- **The physical trend**: boiling point rises regularly with size —
  stronger intermolecular forces need more energy to overcome;
  first four members are gases, mid-range are liquids, solids from
  about C₁₈H₃₈.
- **Combustion**: complete gives CO₂ + H₂O (e.g. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ +
  2H₂O); incomplete gives CO and/or soot instead of CO₂, plus
  water (e.g. 2C₂H₆ + 5O₂ → 4CO + 6H₂O); carbon monoxide is toxic
  because it reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
- **Substitution (4.22)**: alkane + halogen, UV light required;
  one H replaced by one halogen (CH₄ + Br₂ → CH₃Br + HBr);
  products are halogenoalkanes named x-haloalkane; the HCl(g)
  co-product is hydrogen chloride, not hydrochloric acid, until it
  dissolves in water.
:::

:::can-you
- define a hydrocarbon with *only* in place, and an alkane as the
  simplest member of that family?
- state why alkanes are saturated in bonding language — and why
  that saturation explains the family's low reactivity?
- write the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and use it in both directions —
  formula from carbon count, membership from formula?
- draw and name the structural formulae of the first five unbranched
  alkanes, and draw a branched isomer of butane or pentane with
  every bond accounted for?
- reproduce the five-bullet homologous-series definition and deploy
  the one-sentence properties answer?
- explain the boiling-point trend through intermolecular forces and
  place the state boundaries (gases to C₄, solids at about C₁₈H₃₈)?
- derive complete- and incomplete-combustion equations in the fixed
  order and explain why carbon monoxide harms humans?
- give the UV condition for substitution, write the methane–bromine
  and ethane–chlorine equations, and name halogenoalkane products
  correctly?
:::

:::quick-check
If every line of the Can-you checklist above is a confident yes,
you are exam-ready on 4.19–4.22 and the platform bank below is pure
consolidation. If any line wobbled, the fix is surgical: jump back
to that section, reread the key-point box, and retry the worked
example — every section in this lesson was built so that a single
weak link can be re-forged without redoing the family.
:::
